analysis.one_liner: Bans contracts requiring workers to join or pay dues to unions nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so that no worker could ever be required to join a union or pay dues or fees as a condition of employment. It would also let any individual employee sign a personal contract directly with the employer, bypassing the union contract, and it would remove a process that lets workers vote to end a union-security arrangement. Taken together, these changes would make it hard for unions to collect money to operate while letting nonmembers keep union-negotiated pay and benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers would gain leverage, because unions would be financially weakened and any worker could sign an individual deal that undercuts the union contract. Individual employees who object to union dues would stop paying them while still receiving union-negotiated terms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers; workers opposed to union dues

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes every provision of federal labor law that allows union security agreements, meaning no employee could be required to join a union or pay dues or fees as a condition of employment [S2].
It lets an individual employee choose to enter into and administer a personal employment contract with the employer without going through the union bargaining representative [S2][S3].
It repeals the National Labor Relations Board's requirement to hold a secret ballot when 30 percent of employees petition to rescind a union security agreement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Unions would lose dues income while still being legally required to represent all workers in the bargaining unit, making it much harder to fund organizing and bargaining. Workers covered by union contracts would face weaker bargaining power, which research on right-to-work laws links to lower wages over time.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unions and workers in union workplaces

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a free-rider problem: under federal law a union must represent every worker in a bargaining unit, but under this bill no worker would have to pay for that representation, draining union resources [S2].
By allowing individual contracts alongside the collective agreement, the bill would let employers and individual workers cut deals that undermine collectively negotiated wages and conditions [S3].

States with comparable right-to-work laws have generally shown lower union density and, in most economic studies, lower average wages for comparable workers, so a national version would likely weaken pay and bargaining power in unionized workplaces.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A worker who resents paying dues saves money, and no one would be forced to join a union. But the mechanism of the bill is to starve unions of the dues that finance representation while still obligating them to represent everyone, and to open the door to individual contracts that undercut negotiated standards. For workers as a group, the likely cost in bargaining power and wages outweighs the dues saved, which is why organized labor and its allies treated such proposals as an existential threat.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate labor committee and then a subcommittee, and never received any hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the bill in the Senate on November 13, 1991 [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which referred it to the Subcommittee on Labor on November 27, 1991; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, without a committee markup or floor vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, unions kept the ability to negotiate union-security agreements and workers in union workplaces kept their collective bargaining structure; employers did not gain the leverage the bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unions and workers in union workplaces

for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor: introduced the bill to ban union security agreements nationwide

against.name: Committee on Labor and Human Resources (102nd Congress)

against.what_they_did: Took no action: never held a markup or scheduled the bill after referral to its Labor Subcommittee

against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never advanced the bill to a hearing or markup during the 102nd Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape was never tested; the sponsor was a Republican and the Democratic-led labor committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate union security agreements, cutting off dues while unions remain legally required to represent every worker in a bargaining unit. Unions' ability to fund organizing and bargaining runs alongside the wages and benefits of the workers they represent.

Weakened unions and the option of individual contracts would give employers more leverage to hold down wages and set terms directly with individual workers. The employer gain comes at the expense of the union workforce's bargaining power.
